A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same probing study, with matching authors, title, methods and retained English results. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable in both versions and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original classifier evaluations on 16 language models, selectivity measurements, PCA analyses, checkpoint experiments and tokenization comparisons.

after.justification: v3 retains original English experiments and adds multilingual evaluations, attention-output comparisons and activation-steering results.

M1.justification: The core ridge-regression, MLP and random-forest framework remains unchanged. Appendices C–D add auxiliary procedures using averaged attention-head outputs and category-contrast steering vectors to modify classifier inputs.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from English GUM to six languages, adding Chinese, German and French GSD, Russian SynTagRus and Turkish IMST corpora. These datasets introduce substantially different morphological systems while retaining lemma and inflection prediction tasks.

E2.justification: The classifier comparison retains ridge regression, two-layer MLPs and random forests, with random forests still omitted for lemma prediction. Random forests are relocated and discussed further in Appendix E. Added language models expand the analysis targets rather than introduce new competing probing methods.

E3.justification: The model suite expands from 16 to 25, adding Goldfish, mT5-base and Qwen2.5-7B variants. New protocols compare attention and residual outputs and evaluate steering on 1,000 test words at five lambda values using probability change and prediction flip rate. The existing 70/10/20 split is retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds attention-versus-residual analyses and steering sensitivity experiments, and extends separability and category-level error analyses across languages. The earlier tokenization analogy and checkpoint analyses remain, while the accuracy-versus-depth regression analysis in v1 Table 7 is removed.

E5.justification: v1 Table 7 reports fitted regression slopes and R² values for accuracy versus layer depth; v3 removes this statistical trend reporting. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for the experiments.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial multilingual, attention and steering results and removes the regression-trend result table. Reported tokenization statistics also change: BERT's average tokens per word falls from 3.11 to 1.11 in v1 Table 6 versus v3 Table 5. Table 2 and the original English category accuracies remain numerically unchanged.

T1.justification: v3 adds the formal steering-vector construction in Equation 5, contrasting inflection-category means with a weighted average of other categories. The original classifier equations and separability/PCA definitions remain unchanged in substance; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden the encoding claims from 16 models evaluated on English to 25 models across six languages. v3 additionally presents attention localization and effective manipulation of inflectional representations as contributions, and claims the patterns are general rather than language-specific.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations linking language differences to morphological typology, attention outputs to contextual knowledge, and dimensional compression to steering sensitivity. It removes the English-only limitation and explicitly qualifies steering results as changes in classifier predictions rather than downstream model generation.

D1.justification: Section 2.4 newly specifies ridge strength, random-forest search grids, and MLP learning rate, weight decay, epoch limit and early stopping. Table 6 adds exact model identifiers, and Appendices C–D document pooling and steering settings. These disclosures do not establish that retained experiments changed or were rerun.

R1.justification: v3 adds references and discussion concerning multilingual morphology, additional UD corpora, mT5 and intrinsic dimensionality. Section 6 distinguishes its classifier-level steering evaluation from prior output-level interventions. Most existing related-work discussion is retained; the Wolf et al. reference is removed.

P1.justification: Substantial portions of the abstract, Results, Analysis and Conclusion are rewritten around multilingual comparisons. Appendices are reorganized into attention, steering, random-forest and error-analysis sections, while the existing tokenization discussion moves from the main analysis to Appendix B.

P2.justification: v3 combines English linear/MLP accuracy and selectivity into Figure 2 and moves random-forest panels to Figure 13. It adds multilingual, attention and steering plots and extensive multilingual tables. English dataset summaries are consolidated in Figure 5, replacing the earlier sentence-length histogram with summary statistics.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses v1's English-only limitation and supplies valuable experimental details and additional analyses. However, its expanded interpretation is internally inconsistent: Section 4.1 claims MLPs particularly benefit Turkish, while Table 25 reports Turkish mT5 noun accuracy of 0.866 for linear regression versus 0.215 for MLP, and Section 5 gives the opposite classifier ranking. These conflicts affect the strengthened cross-linguistic claims, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.
